stories.headline: AI spots who may get PTSD from what they say in A&E
stories.what: Doctors at NYU Langone let an AI read the stories patients told about why they came to the emergency room, and it flagged every one of 30 people who later developed PTSD.
stories.why: Only about 28 percent of US emergency rooms routinely screen for PTSD, so catching it early could get people help sooner.

stories.headline: A woman with ALS speaks again in her own voice
stories.what: Anne-Marie Poirier, who has ALS, types a few words into the Vocality app and it speaks a full sentence in a voice built from her own recordings.
stories.why: People losing their speech can keep talking to their families in a voice that sounds like them.

stories.headline: AI read 7,800 heart patients' records in a fraction of the time
stories.what: Cleveland Clinic used an AI to review the records of more than 7,800 heart valve patients and predict whose new valve may wear out.
stories.why: Chart review that would have taken doctors years by hand now helps plan each patient's care.

stories.headline: AI could spare one in three lung cancer patients a rushed test
stories.what: Doctors at Memorial Sloan Kettering and Mount Sinai showed an AI reading tissue slides could have let 26 of 80 lung cancer patients skip a rushed gene test without missing anyone who needed it.
stories.why: Fewer rushed tests means faster, cheaper answers and more tissue saved for the full test.

source.label: Clinical Lab Products, AMP 2026 report, 13 Nov 2026

stories.headline: Sensors that give nurses time back raise $5.5 million
stories.what: Akara, a Trinity College Dublin spinout, raised $5.5 million for sensors and AI that track how hospital rooms are used without filming anyone.
stories.why: As much as 40% of nursing time goes on admin, so taking some of it away leaves more time for patients.

source.label: Twilio press release, The AI expectations gap (9 Nov 2026)

sat.hook: Companies: 86% of customers love our AI. Customers: HUMAN. HUMAN. HUMAN.
sat.copy: A meme on Twilio's survey: 86% of companies believe customers are happy with their AI customer service, 51% of customers agree, and 78% have tried to get past the AI to a person. It stands on its own.

pitch.see: Panel one: a smiling executive in front of a chart reading '86% happy'. Panel two: a customer on the phone shouting 'HUMAN' while mashing the zero key.
pitch.lands: Everyone has shouted 'agent' at a phone line; the numbers say they are not alone.
pitch.share: 86% of firms think you love their AI. 78% of you have tried to escape it.

sat.dive: Firms measure their AI on speed while customers judge it on whether they can reach a person, so the two numbers drift apart.
sat.funny: The boardroom chart says delighted; the customer is pressing zero for the ninth time.

lookalike.our_take: Where the post weighs AI against jobs, ours shows the gap between what firms believe and what customers do, and the fix: an easy way to a person.

source.label: National Review, on the Institute for Family Studies poll of 2,000 parents (12 Nov 2026)

sat.hook: 56% of parents want AI blocked at school. Meanwhile, at home:
sat.copy: A meme on the Institute for Family Studies poll: 56% of parents of school-age children want schools to fully block students' use of AI. The joke is the parent who just asked AI to write the email to the school. It stands on its own.

pitch.see: Panel one: a parent at a school meeting, arms folded, under '56% of parents: block AI in schools'. Panel two: the same parent at home, typing 'write a polite email to my son's teacher' into a chatbot.
pitch.lands: Every parent who has used AI for a tricky email will recognise themselves.
pitch.why_now: The poll was reported on 12 Nov 2026.
pitch.share: Ban it at school. Use it for the email to the school.

sat.dive: Most parents want AI kept out of the classroom while using it themselves for the everyday jobs it is good at.
sat.funny: The permission slip banning AI was, of course, drafted by AI.

lookalike.our_take: Where the post weighs AI at work, ours finds the same double standard at the school gate.
